opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that, as an individual contributor, your standard is enforced by your own hands. If something isn't good enough, you just fix it yourself. You stay up late, rewrite the function, refactor the module, and the quality bar holds because you personally hold it. That's actually a very comfortable position, because you never have to have a difficult conversation with anyone.

When you become a manager, that mechanism stops working. You can't rewrite everyone's code, and if you try, you become the bottleneck and the team never grows. So now the standard has to be communicated, and that's a completely different skill. You have to say, "This isn't good enough yet," to someone you like, someone who worked hard on it. Many strong engineers are conflict-averse, and they're also a bit insecure in the new role, so they let things slide. They tell themselves, "It's fine, it's 80% of what I would have done," and that 80% compounds. After a few months, the team's real standard is much lower than the manager's personal standard, and nobody explicitly decided that.

There's another subtle trap. Strong ICs often assume their standard is obvious. To them, it's just "how things should be done," so they never write it down or explain the reasoning. But what's obvious to you came from years of making mistakes. Your teammates haven't made those mistakes yet. So you have to articulate the standard: what good looks like, why it matters, and what the cost is when you fall short. If you can't explain it, you can't scale it.

And honestly, I think the hardest part is emotional. Setting a high standard means you'll sometimes be unpopular in the short term. As an IC, you're judged by your output. As a manager, you're judged by the team's output, and that means being willing to be a little uncomfortable, giving clear, direct feedback early, rather than quietly being disappointed later. I've learned that being kind and having high standards aren't in conflict. The unkind thing is letting someone keep doing mediocre work without telling them, because then they don't grow.

r001.rationale: The response says new managers may avoid difficult conversations and let standards slide, but does not say they model the low-pressure treatment they received as individual contributors.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify greater self-drive than peers as a reason individual contributors were promoted into management.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I went through myself. When I was mostly writing code, my standard was very clear: the code works, it's fast, it's clean. I could look at a pull request and immediately know whether it was good enough. The standard lived in my own hands.

When you become a manager, the thing you're producing is no longer code. It's other people's output, and that's a completely different medium. A lot of strong individual contributors, myself included, make the mistake of thinking the standard is the same, just applied to more people. But you can't apply a code review standard to a person's growth, or to a team's decision-making, or to how a roadmap gets set.

I think there are a few reasons the standard tends to drop rather than rise.

The first one is that you lose the fast feedback loop. As an engineer, you compile, you run tests, you see results in minutes. As a manager, the feedback from a decision might take three months. So you lose the thing that used to calibrate you, and it's really easy to tell yourself "this is probably fine" because nothing is screaming at you right now.

The second one is a kind of empathy trap. Strong ICs usually remember how hard it was to get good. So when they see someone on the team struggling, their instinct is "I was there too, give them time." That's kind, but it's often a way of avoiding the uncomfortable conversation. Setting a high standard means you sometimes have to tell someone that their work is not good enough, and most engineers were never trained to do that. We were trained to just fix it ourselves.

Which brings me to the third problem, and it's the biggest one. When a strong IC sees something below their standard, they know they can fix it in an hour. So they do. And in the short term, the standard looks high, because the output is high. But what you've actually done is lowered the standard for everyone else, because now the team learns that quality is the manager's job. You become the bottleneck, and you're exhausted, and the team never develops its own taste.

Setting a high standard as a manager is really about building taste in other people. That means you have to articulate what good looks like out loud, in words, repeatedly, instead of just knowing it in your gut. A lot of us never had to put that into language before. I remember trying to explain why one design was better than another and realizing I couldn't say it clearly. I just felt it. And if you can't say it, you can't scale it.

So my honest answer is that strong ICs don't struggle because they lack standards. They struggle because their standards are tacit, they're used to enforcing them with their own hands, and they're uncomfortable with the slower, more human process of making other people own them. The ones who get past it are the people who accept that their job changed, and that the new job is harder in a way their old skills didn't prepare them for.

r001.rationale: The response says managers may remember how hard it was to improve and give struggling teammates more time, but it does not say they model the low-pressure treatment they received as individual contributors.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention greater self-drive than peers as a reason individual contributors are promoted to management.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that, as an individual contributor, you have a very direct way to maintain a high standard: you do the work yourself. You notice something is wrong, and you fix it. When you become a manager, that instinct can actually get in the way. You keep stepping in, and the team never develops its own judgment.

The harder thing is to make your standards explicit. What does good work look like? Why does this detail matter? Which tradeoffs are acceptable? Something that feels obvious to you may come from years of experience that the other person hasn’t had yet.

And then there’s the discomfort of giving feedback. You can know technically that something isn’t good enough and still hesitate to tell someone that. So I think the transition is about learning to be demanding and supportive at the same time: being clear about the gap, while helping the person build the ability to close it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses stepping in, making standards explicit, and giving feedback, but does not say new managers model the low-pressure treatment they received as contributors.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention that individual contributors were promoted because they were more self-driven than their peers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think when you’re a strong individual contributor, your standard is often implicit. You look at something and you know it’s not good enough, and then you fix it yourself. But as a manager, you have to make that judgment explicit: What does good look like? Why does it matter? How can someone else get there?

And there’s a social challenge. Giving direct feedback can feel uncomfortable, especially when you know people are working hard. So you might accept work you wouldn’t accept from yourself, or quietly redo it. That solves the immediate problem, but it doesn’t help the team improve.

The shift is to hold a high standard while giving people the context, feedback, and support to meet it. Your own performance is no longer enough. You have to help other people develop the judgment that made you effective.

r001.rationale: The response says managers may avoid direct feedback or redo work themselves, but does not say they model the low-pressure treatment they received as individual contributors.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention that individual contributors were promoted because they were more self-driven than their former peers.
